paragraphs: Data valuation assigns scores to individual data sources according to their usefulness for training a model. Those scores can themselves create privacy concerns. This paper examines that problem for KNN-Shapley, a practical valuation method, showing both its inherent privacy risks and the technical difficulty of adding differential privacy directly.

The authors introduce TKNN-Shapley, a revised valuation method designed to make privacy protection easier to incorporate. Its differentially private version, DP-TKNN-Shapley, offers a better balance between privacy and useful valuation results than a straightforward private adaptation of KNN-Shapley. The contribution therefore concerns the design of the underlying valuation procedure as well as its privacy protection.

The authors also compare the methods without privacy protection: TKNN-Shapley matches KNN-Shapley at distinguishing data quality. Together, these findings suggest that changing the valuation method can make privacy protection more practical while retaining useful quality assessments. The privacy guarantee belongs to the explicitly private variant; the non-private comparison establishes the usefulness of the revised scoring method.
neurips-2023-a-privacy-friendly-approach.tldr: TKNN-Shapley redesigns data valuation to support differential privacy with a better privacy–utility tradeoff than naively privatizing KNN-Shapley.

paragraphs: Reducing numerical precision can shrink large translation models, but pushing weights and activations down to one bit changes how their computations behave. This paper introduces BMT, a binarization technique for Transformer machine translation models. It identifies inflated variation in dot products as a particular problem when both weights and activations use one-bit representations.

BMT adds normalization layers and residual connections to improve the quality of binarized models. These architectural changes address the behavior of the compressed computations rather than treating binarization purely as a storage conversion. The paper distinguishes weight-only binarization from binarizing activations too, because the two choices have different effects on translation quality.

On WMT, a Transformer with one-bit weights matches the quality of a floating-point model while being 16 times smaller. One-bit activations still cause varying quality losses, although the changes reduce them. A separate scaling study on production-scale translation datasets finds that one-bit weight models scale and generalize well within and beyond their training domain. These results support weight binarization while preserving the reported activation-quality tradeoff.
neurips-2023-binarized-neural-machine-tr.tldr: BMT enables one-bit Transformer weights to match floating-point translation quality in reported experiments, while architectural changes reduce losses from one-bit activations.

paragraphs: A first-person camera records only part of the environment at any moment, even though the wearer acts within a persistent physical space. Video features built from short clips can lose that wider context. EgoEnv learns representations that connect the video to the wearer's local surroundings, including surroundings that may not currently be visible.

The models learn from agents moving through simulated three-dimensional environments, where the full environment is available during training. This setting supplies information about the surroundings that a camera view alone cannot provide. The learned representations are then tested on real videos captured by humans in environments that were not seen during training.

Across two human-centric video tasks, adding these environment-aware features consistently improves results over corresponding models using traditional clip features. Despite training exclusively on simulated video, the approach works on HouseTours and Ego4D footage and achieves state-of-the-art results on the Ego4D NLQ challenge. The findings show that learning about persistent surroundings in simulation can provide useful context for understanding real first-person video.
neurips-2023-egoenv-human-centric-enviro.tldr: EgoEnv learns surrounding-environment features from simulated first-person video that improve understanding of real human-captured video.

paragraphs: In long-tailed classification, some categories have many training examples while others have very few. Image mixing can strengthen the representation of rare categories by creating additional synthetic examples. However, randomly combining a foreground from a rare category with a background from a common category can ignore whether the individual images make sense together.

This paper proposes adaptive mixing based on optimal transport. The method considers information about both the categories and the individual samples when constructing mixed images. Its purpose is to produce semantically reasonable training examples for minority categories, making the choice of image combinations part of the augmentation method rather than leaving it random.

Experiments report effective performance on long-tailed classification tasks. The method can also be combined with existing approaches to improve their performance, so its role is not restricted to a standalone classifier. The authors additionally describe its use as general augmentation for balanced datasets. The central contribution is a way to account for sample compatibility while increasing the training presence of underrepresented categories.
neurips-2023-enhancing-minority-classes-.tldr: Adaptive optimal-transport image mixing uses category and sample information to create useful training examples for underrepresented classes.

paragraphs: Imitation learning tries to reproduce expert behavior from demonstrations without requiring an explicit reward signal. Real demonstrations can contain several distinct behaviors, with some appearing much more frequently than others. Labeling those behaviors can also be expensive. Ess-InfoGAIL addresses these problems together by learning separated behavior representations from imbalanced demonstrations with only limited labeled data.

The architecture combines three mechanisms. It adapts semi-supervised generative adversarial learning to imitation, allowing labeled and unlabeled demonstrations to contribute. It also learns a latent distribution to align generated behavior with the expert data distribution. Finally, regularized information maximization works with an approximate prior over labels to improve learning from the limited supervision.

These components make the distribution of behavior types part of what the system learns, while using the available labels to help distinguish behaviors. Experiments report efficient learning of multiple behavior modes from imbalanced demonstrations relative to baseline methods. The stated contribution is therefore a combined approach to behavioral diversity, unequal demonstration counts, and limited labeling, rather than an assumption that every behavior has abundant labeled examples.
neurips-2023-ess-infogail-semi-supervise.tldr: Ess-InfoGAIL combines semi-supervised adversarial learning and a learned behavior distribution to imitate diverse experts from imbalanced, sparsely labeled demonstrations.

paragraphs: Federated learning must often combine learning across clients whose data follow different distributions. Sharing information between clients can help with these differences, but it also creates tension between model performance and privacy. FedFed investigates whether sharing only part of the features in the data can help address this problem.

The method divides features according to their contribution to model performance. Features that contribute strongly are called performance-sensitive and are shared globally. Features with a more limited contribution are called performance-robust and remain local. Clients then train using both their local data and the shared information. Here, sensitivity describes importance for prediction, rather than being a designation of how private a feature is.

Comprehensive experiments show that FedFed improves model performance. The approach matters because it makes the selection of shared information an explicit part of handling differences among clients. Its stated result supports partial feature sharing as a useful strategy for federated learning, with the separation between shared and local features organized around their contribution to the learning task.
neurips-2023-fedfed-feature-distillation.tldr: FedFed improves federated learning by sharing features that strongly contribute to performance while keeping less influential features local.

paragraphs: Matrix sensing over graphs generalizes matrix completion and matrix sensing, but the existing analyses do not directly cover this broader problem. This paper studies its optimization landscape: the structure that determines whether an optimization method can reach a globally correct solution or encounter troublesome stationary points.

The authors introduce a condition called Ω-RIP to characterize optimization complexity. They combine it with an improved regularizer for incoherence, a property imposed in their analysis. Under both the incoherence and Ω-RIP conditions, they prove that the problem has the strict saddle property with high probability. This structure supports methods designed to avoid saddles, giving those methods polynomial-time global convergence guarantees.

The conditions are central to the result: the guarantee applies to the analyzed setting when those requirements hold. The authors report bounds that are tight up to a constant compared with state-of-the-art results. Numerical illustrations also show a close relationship between Ω-RIP and optimization complexity, connecting the new theoretical condition to observed optimization behavior.
neurips-2023-geometric-analysis-of-matri.tldr: A new Ω-RIP condition supports conditional guarantees that saddle-avoiding methods solve matrix sensing over graphs in polynomial time.

paragraphs: Pruning followed by additional training often produces smaller models that still generalize well, but explaining that success theoretically is difficult. This paper studies the process in matrix sensing, where the trained representation has many more columns than the ground-truth representation needs. It analyzes approximate local minima of squared error with a smoothed group Lasso penalty.

The penalty acts on entire columns. The authors prove that removing columns whose norms fall below an explicit threshold leaves exactly the minimum required number of columns, while keeping training loss close to the ground-truth solution. Starting gradient descent from this pruned representation then gives linear convergence to its limit during fine-tuning.

The analysis also explains why regularization matters for this pruning rule. Without it, gradient descent can produce many columns with comparable norms, making small-column removal unsuitable. The results extend to two-layer neural networks with quadratic activations. These findings provide rigorous support for pruning and fine-tuning in the studied settings, showing how regularization can make redundant structure identifiable through a simple magnitude threshold.
neurips-2023-greedy-pruning-with-group-l.tldr: For matrix sensing, group Lasso makes norm-based pruning recover the required model size and supports provably effective fine-tuning.

paragraphs: In a teacher–student experiment, a student network learns from data generated by a fixed teacher. When the student is larger, a natural question is whether its learned ability resides in a smaller substructure resembling the teacher. This paper investigates that question using a different way to optimize information transfer between network layers.

The method represents those linear transfers spectrally and computes gradients with respect to both eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The authors report negligible additional computational and complexity costs compared with standard training. In this framework, they isolate a stable student substructure that reflects the teacher's complexity in its number of computing neurons, distribution of paths, and topology.

The optimized eigenvalues also supply a ranking for removing unimportant nodes. In the reported observations, pruning causes no performance degradation while the remaining size stays above a threshold corresponding to the teacher's effective size. The authors describe the observed transition using a second-order phase-transition interpretation with universality traits. The findings connect the training representation to the discovery and removal of excess network structure.
neurips-2023-how-a-student-becomes-a-tea.tldr: Spectral training reveals a stable teacher-like substructure inside larger student networks and enables pruning without observed performance loss above a size threshold.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization means handling new combinations of underlying factors, rather than only combinations encountered during training. This paper draws inspiration from iterated learning, a cognitive-science account of how language might develop that ability. The account combines pressure to make representations easy for a new learner to acquire with pressure to keep them expressive enough for useful tasks.

The proposed approach applies iterated learning to neural networks with simplicial embeddings. These embeddings make representations approximately discrete, giving the learning process a particular structure on which to operate. An analysis based on Kolmogorov complexity further motivates the approach by relating compositionality to how compactly a representation can be described.

The combined changes improve compositional generalization over other approaches in the reported experiments. The authors demonstrate gains on vision tasks with understood latent factors and on real molecular graph prediction tasks whose latent structure is unknown. The second setting matters because it extends the empirical evidence beyond tasks where the underlying factors are already clear to the experimenter.
neurips-2023-improving-compositional-gen.tldr: Iterated learning with approximately discrete simplicial embeddings improves generalization to unseen combinations in vision and molecular graph tasks.

paragraphs: A multi-armed bandit repeatedly chooses among actions with uncertain rewards, balancing learning about them against collecting reward. This paper studies rewards bounded between zero and one. It analyzes KL-MS, a Kullback–Leibler extension of Maillard sampling, whose closed-form action probabilities are useful for evaluating policies from previously collected data.

The analysis gives a finite-time regret bound that depends on reward gaps, meaning differences between the quality of the best action and the alternatives. For Bernoulli rewards, the authors also prove asymptotic optimality. That guarantee concerns behavior over long horizons in the Bernoulli setting, while the paper's broader problem formulation allows reward distributions throughout the bounded interval.

A further worst-case bound adapts to the best action's mean reward. Its leading square-root term includes the factor μ*(1−μ*), together with the number of actions, time horizon, and a logarithmic factor; an additional term scales with the number of actions times log time. This makes the guarantee sensitive to the best mean's proximity to the interval's endpoints. The contribution combines that adaptivity with the stated asymptotic guarantee.
neurips-2023-kullback-leibler-maillard-s.tldr: KL-MS combines explicit action probabilities with bounded-reward regret guarantees that adapt to the best mean and are asymptotically optimal for Bernoulli rewards.

paragraphs: Recovering causal relationships among hidden variables is difficult when neither the variables nor the interventions affecting them are directly known. This paper establishes conditions under which latent causal graphs in measurement models can nevertheless be identified and reconstructed. The results avoid specifying parametric forms such as linear relationships or Gaussian distributions.

The analysis also does not require knowing the number of hidden variables in advance. Under the established conditions, at most one unknown intervention per hidden variable is needed. The proofs are constructive, connecting the identification claims to reconstruction, and introduce two graphical concepts called imaginary subsets and isolated edges as part of the argument.

The paper additionally characterizes limits on which edge directions can be determined within classes of directed acyclic graphs compatible with unknown interventions. This places orientation ambiguity within the theory itself. The contribution is a set of conditional identification results without parametric assumptions or faithfulness, rather than an unconditional claim that any hidden causal graph can be recovered from unknown interventions.
neurips-2023-learning-nonparametric-late.tldr: The paper establishes conditions for reconstructing hidden causal graphs from unknown interventions without parametric assumptions or knowing the number of hidden variables.

paragraphs: Inverse constrained reinforcement learning seeks to infer the constraints that experts respect from their demonstrations. A single constraint function becomes difficult to justify when the demonstrations mix experts operating under different restrictions. MMICRL addresses this setting by estimating multiple sets of constraints corresponding to different expert types.

The method uses a flow-based density estimator to identify experts without expert labels, then infers constraints specific to those agents. To imitate their behavior, it combines constrained policy optimization with opposing entropy objectives: lower entropy when conditioned on an agent and higher entropy across agents. This encourages coherent behavior for each type while retaining diversity in the overall collection of policies.

The authors integrate this objective into a contrastive learning framework to improve robustness. Experiments in discrete and continuous environments report better constraint recovery and control performance than baseline methods. The significance is that behavioral differences can be represented through distinct constraints and policies, allowing imitation to preserve variation among experts instead of explaining the entire demonstration mixture through one shared constraint function.
neurips-2023-multi-modal-inverse-constra.tldr: MMICRL identifies expert types without labels and learns their distinct constraints and policies from mixed demonstrations.

paragraphs: Online list labeling stores arriving items in sorted order inside an array whose size is proportional to the number of items. An item's array position serves as its label. Inserting new items can require moving existing ones, so the goal is to minimize those moves while continuously maintaining sorted order.

This paper designs a data structure that uses predictions and analyzes how its performance depends on their errors. In a worst-case model, it provides guarantees optimal for any prediction error while retaining the best-known worst-case bound even when predictions are entirely wrong. This combines the possibility of gains from useful forecasts with a stated fallback guarantee under unreliable ones.

The authors also study a stochastic error model, bounding performance using the error's expectation and variance. Empirical results support the theoretical analysis on real temporal datasets, where predictions are built from previously arrived elements. That setup connects the analysis to a practical forecasting pattern: past arrivals supply information for future insertions without requiring predictions to be perfect.
neurips-2023-online-list-labeling-with-p.tldr: A prediction-aware sorted-array data structure gains error-dependent guarantees while retaining the best-known worst-case bound when predictions fail.

paragraphs: Regression models predict numerical labels, and those labels may need privacy protection during training. This paper develops a family of label randomizers for regression under label differential privacy. The design problem is to alter labels enough to satisfy the privacy requirement while preserving information useful for learning the prediction task.

The authors use the tradeoff between bias and variance to construct the randomizers. Bias concerns systematic distortion, while variance concerns the spread introduced by randomness. Their construction depends on a prior distribution over labels that is itself estimated privately. This allows the randomization procedure to respond to the label distribution while accounting for privacy in estimating that distribution.

Across several datasets, the randomizers achieve state-of-the-art privacy–utility tradeoffs. The results highlight the importance of reducing bias when neural networks learn under label privacy constraints. Alongside the experiments, the paper provides theoretical results about the structural properties of optimal unbiased randomizers. Together, the findings connect useful private regression performance to deliberate control of the statistical distortion introduced into labels.
neurips-2023-optimal-unbiased-randomizer.tldr: Privately estimated label distributions guide regression randomizers that improve privacy–utility tradeoffs by managing bias and variance.

paragraphs: This paper reconstructs a smooth surface from an unordered collection of points sampled from a closed surface. It seeks to preserve geometry using only those points, without requiring surface normals or ground-truth values of an implicit function. The approach uses mathematical constraints on a learned representation to supply the needed supervision.

The model learns a signed distance function through a formulation based on the p-Poisson equation. The reconstructed surface consists of locations where this function is zero. For efficient training, the method introduces an auxiliary variable representing the function's gradient and enforces the equation directly on that variable as a hard constraint.

The method also constrains the auxiliary field to be curl-free, reflecting a fundamental property of gradient fields. The authors report that this produces more faithful reconstructions. Experiments on standard benchmarks show superior and robust surface reconstruction. The result supports the sufficiency of the proposed equation and vector-field supervision in the studied setting, where the input points come from a closed surface and no additional geometric annotations are supplied.
neurips-2023-p-poisson-surface-reconstru.tldr: A neural signed distance representation uses p-Poisson and curl-free constraints to reconstruct closed surfaces from point clouds without normals.

paragraphs: Learning a scene as a collection of points requires finding both useful point locations and a way to turn them into images. Existing point-based approaches can struggle with vanishing gradients or need many points to capture geometry and texture. PAPR combines a point-based scene representation with a differentiable renderer to address these difficulties.

Each point carries a spatial position, an influence score, and a feature vector that does not depend on viewing direction. For each viewing ray, the renderer selects relevant points and uses their features to produce a color. This links the image-producing process to the point representation so that learning can adjust the scene geometry.

The authors show that PAPR learns appropriate point positions even when its initialization differs substantially from the target geometry. It also captures fine texture with a compact collection of points. Demonstrated applications include zero-shot geometry editing, object manipulation, texture transfer, and exposure control. These results connect the learned representation's rendering quality with its usefulness for manipulating different aspects of a scene.
neurips-2023-papr-proximity-attention-po.tldr: PAPR learns compact point-based scenes with accurate geometry and fine texture using a differentiable renderer that selects relevant points for each ray.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories to image pixels, but a good aggregate score can obscure uneven performance. Frequent classes contribute more observations, and large objects occupy more pixels than small ones. This paper examines how those two imbalances affect common metrics, including measures that already average performance across classes.

The authors propose fine-grained mean intersection-over-union measures together with corresponding worst-case metrics. Their purpose is to reduce bias toward large objects and reveal more about the distribution of performance. This provides additional information for auditing datasets and models, beyond a single score that compresses different kinds of success and failure into one number.

The study trains and evaluates 15 modern networks on 12 natural and aerial segmentation datasets. Its findings confirm reduced large-object bias and support evaluating models with multiple metrics. The authors also identify architecture and loss-function choices as important for optimizing the fine-grained measures. Thus, the contribution addresses both how segmentation quality is assessed and how training choices relate to the more detailed assessment.
neurips-2023-revisiting-evaluation-metri.tldr: Fine-grained segmentation metrics reduce large-object bias and reveal performance differences hidden by conventional aggregate scores.

paragraphs: Learning through an optimal-control solver requires understanding how its optimized trajectory changes when inputs or parameters change. This paper develops a method for computing those derivatives in non-convex, constrained, discrete-time control problems. It uses the implicit function theorem applied to the equations describing an optimal solution.

Earlier approaches solve a differentiated optimality system through an auxiliary linear quadratic regulator problem. The proposed method instead eliminates the Lagrange multiplier terms and directly evaluates the resulting matrix equations. By exploiting their structure, it makes trajectory-derivative computation scale linearly with the number of timesteps. It also supports parallelization and direct vector–Jacobian products, which provide combined derivative information useful in learning.

The authors report improved numerical stability and scalability with model size relative to prior work. Their analysis also unifies earlier methods and addresses claims that implicit-function-based differentiation must scale quadratically with trajectory length. Evaluation includes a synthetic benchmark and four learning-from-demonstration benchmarks, including six-degree-of-freedom quadrotor maneuvering and rocket-powered landing. The contribution is a more structured computation of derivatives through the control solution.
neurips-2023-revisiting-implicit-differe.tldr: Structured elimination of optimality equations enables scalable, numerically improved differentiation through constrained optimal-control trajectories.

paragraphs: Reward-directed generation aims to produce samples with desired properties expressed through a reward function. This paper studies a setting with mostly unlabeled data and a small collection of noisy reward labels. It asks how a conditional diffusion model can use that limited supervision to generate samples associated with a requested reward.

The approach first learns a reward predictor from the labeled subset and uses it to assign predicted labels to the remaining data. A conditional diffusion model then trains on the resulting dataset. At generation time, a user-specified target reward becomes the conditioning value, directing the sampling process toward that target.

The theoretical analysis shows that the generator can recover the data's latent subspace and learn the reward-conditioned distribution, producing samples that move closer to the requested target. Reward improvement depends on the strength of the reward signal, distribution shift, and the cost of extrapolating beyond the data's support. Empirical results validate the theory and examine how stronger extrapolation relates to sample quality, preserving an explicit tradeoff in directing generation toward desired outcomes.
neurips-2023-reward-directed-conditional.tldr: Reward pseudolabels train conditional diffusion models to target desired outcomes, with theoretical gains shaped by signal strength and extrapolation costs.

paragraphs: Data valuation ranks training examples by their contribution, but randomness in the utility being measured can make those rankings unstable. Earlier work favored the Banzhaf value for robustness without assuming a particular noise structure. This paper finds empirically that it is not always the most robust choice within the broader weighted Banzhaf family.

The authors introduce Kronecker noise as a way to describe the structure of that randomness. Within this framework, they derive a uniquely robust semi-value from the noise and show that it belongs to the weighted Banzhaf family while minimizing worst-case entropy. The theoretical preference therefore depends on the modeled noise structure rather than selecting one weighting independently of the noise.

They also develop an estimator that reuses samples extensively and has the stated best time complexity for a specified approximation guarantee. Tests use synthetic and authentic noise. For authentic noise, the method fits the Kronecker model and uses it to predict the most robust semi-value. The results support adapting valuation weights to stochasticity when reliable data rankings are difficult to obtain.
neurips-2023-robust-data-valuation-with-.tldr: Weighted Banzhaf values can improve data-ranking robustness by adapting the valuation rule to a modeled noise structure.

paragraphs: HUME approaches unsupervised learning as a search for labels that agree across different representations of the same dataset. Its motivating observation is that many human-defined categories can be separated by linear classifiers in different representation spaces. A candidate labeling that remains easy to separate across spaces can therefore provide evidence of an underlying human labeling.

The framework keeps pretrained representations fixed and trains only linear classifiers on top of them. Its objective guides the search over candidate labelings without external supervision for that search. The authors find that the objective correlates strongly with the dataset's ground-truth labeling. Because it operates on fixed representations, the framework is compatible with large pretrained and self-supervised models.

On STL-10, HUME substantially outperforms a supervised linear classifier using self-supervised representations, while achieving comparable results on CIFAR-10. It also reports state-of-the-art unsupervised results on four image classification benchmarks, including ImageNet-1000. These findings support consistency across representation spaces as a useful signal for discovering categories, with the reported supervised comparisons tied to their particular datasets and classifier setup.
neurips-2023-the-pursuit-of-human-labeli.tldr: HUME discovers labels without external supervision by searching for labelings that linear classifiers can consistently recover across fixed representation spaces.

paragraphs: Machine learning for catalyst modeling has often focused on predicting energy, while significant generalization beyond the training distribution has remained difficult to demonstrate. This paper investigates predicting Kohn–Sham charge density point by point instead. Charge density provides a different learning target within the physical framework underlying many catalyst applications.

The authors introduce a dataset of bulk catalysts with charge densities and test whether density models handle new structures containing element combinations absent from training. They show this form of combinatorial generalization in their experiments. The relevant novelty is the combination of elements, making the evaluation directly connected to prediction across unfamiliar chemical combinations.

The learned densities also help Density Functional Theory calculations converge: more than 80% of binary and ternary test cases converge faster than standard baselines, with an average 13% reduction in iteration count. The paper explicitly recognizes greater inference costs for density learning. Its results suggest a viable alternative that trades those costs for progress on combinatorial generalization and reduced iteration requirements in the evaluated calculations.
neurips-2023-towards-combinatorial-gener.tldr: Learning catalyst charge densities generalizes to unseen element combinations in reported tests and reduces DFT iterations, at greater inference cost.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from existing transitions without access to the real dynamics, and its estimates of future value can diverge during training. This paper identifies self-excitation as the primary mechanism behind that instability. It introduces SEEM, a measure based on the neural tangent kernel, to track properties of the value network as training evolves.

The theory can identify divergence early and, when stochastic gradient descent is used, predict the growth order of estimated values and model norms as well as the crashing step. The authors report experimental agreement with these predictions. This moves the discussion from associating instability with unfamiliar actions toward a mechanism that can be measured during training.

The resulting remedy focuses on network architecture and extrapolation behavior. Extensive experiments identify LayerNorm as effective at avoiding divergence without introducing detrimental bias. The authors report success even in challenging settings using only 1% of dataset transitions, where previous methods fail, and state-of-the-art results when integrating it into modern offline methods. These are reported empirical outcomes across the evaluated settings.
neurips-2023-understanding-predicting-an.tldr: A self-excitation analysis predicts offline value divergence and motivates LayerNorm as an empirically effective architectural remedy.

paragraphs: Predicting physical systems on unstructured meshes requires handling both their evolving state and, in many cases, meaningful stochastic variation. This paper proposes one framework for deterministic and stochastic rollouts. It combines compact physical representations with a generative sequence model, allowing predictions to describe multiple possible evolutions.

An autoencoder first compresses the full physical variables into a lower-dimensional representation. A transformer then works with a conditional normalizing flow to model sequences in that reduced space. This divides the task into representing the physical state compactly and learning how the resulting representations evolve over time, including variation in possible future states.

On deterministic systems, the model produces more accurate predictions than several competitive baselines, and its uncertainty estimates reflect its own prediction error. On stochastic systems, it generates high-quality rollout samples whose means and variances closely match those from expensive numerical simulations. The findings support the combined architecture for both kinds of dynamics, with the stochastic evaluation assessing distributional statistics as well as the quality of individual generated trajectories.
neurips-2023-unifying-predictions-of-det.tldr: A compact-state transformer and conditional flow improve deterministic physics predictions and generate stochastic rollouts with realistic means and variances.
